king gizzard & the lizard wizard|fishing.fact: King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard's title track "Fishing for Fishies" is a warped nursery rhyme against recreational fishing - when asked what inspired the 2019 album's title, Stu Mackenzie simply wrote, "hunting makes me sad." Its music video, directed by Jason Galea, has the band floating on a raft past an alligator playing electric piano.

rilo kiley|science vs. romance.fact: Rilo Kiley's "Science Vs. Romance," from 2001's Take Offs and Landings, was written by Jenny Lewis and Blake Sennett - Stereogum later ranked it among the band's ten best songs.

mitski|i'll change for you.fact: Mitski's "I'll Change for You," the second single from 2026's Nothing's About to Happen to Me, came from wanting to write "a song about being pathetic" - channeling the irrational urge to beg an ex to take you back, in Mitski's own words.

sufjan stevens|with my whole heart.fact: Sufjan Stevens released "With My Whole Heart" alongside "Love Yourself" as a Pride Month single in 2019, with proceeds from companion T-shirts going to organizations supporting LGBTQ youth.

pavement|spit on a stranger.fact: Pavement's "Spit on a Stranger" opens 1999's Terror Twilight, the band's Nigel Godrich-produced final album - its single also included the deep cut "Harness Your Hopes," which years later, thanks to Spotify's algorithm, unexpectedly became the band's most-streamed song.

real estate|crime.fact: Real Estate's "Crime" comes from their self-titled 2009 debut, which Pitchfork gave an 8.5 and its Best New Music tag - an early sign of the acclaim the Ridgewood, New Jersey band would keep earning.

band of horses|the great salt lake.fact: Band of Horses' "The Great Salt Lake," from 2006's Everything All the Time, isn't really about the Great Salt Lake at all - frontman Ben Bridwell has said the imagery mostly pulls from Lake Murray, a reservoir in his home state of South Carolina, mixed with stories about friends from Salt Lake City.

sweeping promises|accent.fact: Sweeping Promises' "Accent," from 2026's You Say I Romanticize, is built around what the band calls a "cicadence" - a flapping, insectoid post-punk rhythm - wrestling with the uneasy feeling of trying to express yourself in a world that can make you feel like you're speaking a foreign language.

spiritualized|ladies & gentlemen we are.fact: Spiritualized's title track "Ladies and Gentlemen We Are Floating in Space" borrows its melody from both Pachelbel's Canon in D and Elvis Presley's "Can't Help Falling in Love" - the album opens with band member Kate Radley's flat, deadpan voice on a phone recording saying the title phrase. NME ranked the 1997 album its #1 record of the year, ahead of Radiohead's OK Computer.

sparks|the number one song in heaven.fact: Sparks' "The Number One Song in Heaven" was written and produced with Giorgio Moroder after the Mael brothers heard his production on Donna Summer's "I Feel Love" and decided to ditch their guitars for synthesizers - it became a UK top-20 hit and, in 1997, was re-recorded with vocals from Bronski Beat's Jimmy Somerville.

beirut|gallipoli.fact: Beirut's title track "Gallipoli" came from a chance encounter - Zach Condon stumbled into a brass band procession carrying a saint's statue through the Italian town of Gallipoli, with church bells ringing and the band's sound bouncing off the narrow streets. He wrote the entire song the next day in one sitting, pausing only to eat.

cake|comfort eagle.fact: CAKE's title track "Comfort Eagle" is more widely known by its repeated hook, "Building a Religion" - frontman John McCrea wrote it as a metaphor for the marketing and propaganda that disguises what a product actually is. Fans voted it in as the album's second single, but its release was canceled after the September 11 attacks.

father john misty|pure comedy.fact: Father John Misty's title track "Pure Comedy" first previewed live at a December 2016 benefit concert for Seattle Children's Hospital - its opening verse is an almost direct paraphrase of an unplanned rant he delivered on stage at a festival earlier that year.

pickwick|turncoat.fact: Pickwick's "Turncoat" was the lead single from 2017's LoveJoys - the band's first album with producer Erik Blood, whose experimental tinkering pushed their sound toward a more psychedelic, kinetic direction.

toro y moi|so many details.fact: Toro y Moi's "So Many Details," the lead single from 2013's Anything in Return, was written, produced, and performed entirely by Chaz Bundick himself - Pitchfork called it a leap forward in his songwriting after his move from South Carolina to Berkeley, California.

wild nothing|only heather.fact: Wild Nothing's "Only Heather" comes from 2012's Nocturne - Jack Tatum's second album under the Wild Nothing name, which he began recording alone in Blacksburg, Virginia back in 2009.

twisted teens|when we first met.fact: Twisted Teens' "When We First Met" comes from The Holy Cross Tigers on Sub Pop - the New Orleans garage-punk duo of Caspian Hollywell and Ramon "RJ" Santos blend the street-level grit of The Gun Club with early-punk urgency and dusty country-blues storytelling.

king tuff|landline.fact: King Tuff's "Landline," from 2026's MOO, was recorded entirely on his Tascam 338 tape machine - the same one he used on his very first album, Was Dead, years earlier.

belle and sebastian|i don't know what yo.fact: Belle and Sebastian's "I Don't Know What You See In Me" marked a first for the band - their first-ever co-write with an outside songwriter, Scottish producer Wuh Oh (Peter Ferguson), on the lead single from 2023's Late Developers.

squid|paddling.fact: Squid's "Paddling," from 2021's Bright Green Field, was a longtime live staple years before its release - the band started writing it back when they were still teenagers living in Brighton, and it explores the tension between simple pleasures and modern consumerism through the lens of The Wind in the Willows.

diiv|kid.fact: DIIV's "Kid" comes from 2012's Oshin, the band's shoegaze-leaning debut - frontman Zachary Cole Smith has said Malian guitarist Baba Salah's record Borey shaped how he approached melody on the album.

ramones|gimme gimme shock treatment.fact: Ramones' "Gimme Gimme Shock Treatment," from 1977's Leave Home, was written by Dee Dee and Johnny Ramone at artist Arturo Vega's loft - the title nods to electroconvulsive therapy, filtered through the band's usual dark, satirical humor rather than anything to be taken literally.

beck|run away.fact: Beck's "Run Away," from 2026's Ride Lonesome, was mixed by longtime collaborator Nigel Godrich - its Tokyo-set music video stars Golden Globe-winning actor Tadanobu Asano, known for roles in Shogun and Thor: Ragnarok.

courtney barnett|need a little time.fact: Courtney Barnett's "Need a Little Time," the second single from 2018's Tell Me How You Really Feel, is about needing space in a relationship - its music video, directed by Danny Cohen, follows Barnett as a cosmic traveler morphing through time and space.

r.e.m.|daysleeper.fact: R.E.M.'s "Daysleeper" was the first single from 1998's Up - Michael Stipe wrote the lyrics after noticing the word "Daysleeper" on an apartment door and wondering about the life of the person living behind it. The music itself had actually been written years earlier, during the New Adventures in Hi-Fi sessions, but sat unused until Stipe found words for it.

wishy|sensational.fact: Wishy's "Sensational" grew out of a bassline Mitch Collins kept noodling on during soundchecks - it's a stylistic left turn from their earlier singles on 2026's Nature's Pill, its music video built from an animated collage of 3,000 cut-outs of the band.

the modern lovers|astral plane.fact: The Modern Lovers' "Astral Plane" was produced by John Cale of the Velvet Underground during their mid-1970s demo sessions - Jonathan Richman's lyrics turn a rejected pickup line into a promise to meet someone on a higher plane of existence instead.

stephen malkmus and the jicks|real emoti.fact: Stephen Malkmus and the Jicks' title track "Real Emotional Trash" stretches past ten minutes, built around an extended midsection of interlocking guitar solos - the album was recorded at SnowGhost Music in Whitefish, Montana, and Foxtrot Studio in Chicago.

kevin morby|i have been to the mountain.fact: Kevin Morby's "I Have Been to the Mountain," from 2016's Singing Saw, is one of his most richly orchestrated songs - built around mariachi horns, an angelic choir, and psychedelic guitar, recorded with Sam Cohen in Woodstock, New York after Morby started writing on an old piano that came with a new house.

elastica|stutter.fact: Elastica's debut single "Stutter" sold out its limited 1,500-copy pressing in a single day and shot to #1 on the UK indie charts - on the strength of just that one single and a couple of gigs, the band was voted Best New Band in Melody Maker's year-end readers' poll.

bat for lashes|the hunger.fact: Bat for Lashes' "The Hunger," from 2019's Lost Girls, started with an old '80s synth organ sound Natasha Khan was playing around with before co-writer/producer Charles Scott IV added bass - the whole album grew out of a screenplay Khan had been writing, inspired by '80s vampire and coming-of-age films.

soccer mommy|rings of saturn.fact: Soccer Mommy's "Rings of Saturn" was Sophie Allison's first new song in two years, produced by Elliott Kozel - she's said she wrote it during a hard stretch when she'd take a telescope out into the yard to look at the moon and planets, finding that feeling small could take some of the weight off.

jungle|i've been in love (feat. channel.fact: Jungle's "I've Been In Love," featuring Channel Tres, comes from 2023's Volcano - bandmember Josh Lloyd-Watson has called it "the most honest record" Jungle has made, an extension of the group's long-running love for soul music.

chvrches|roses.fact: Chvrches' "Roses" marked the band's first new music in three years - the chorus interpolates the old English nursery rhyme "Ring a Ring o' Roses," folded into a heavier, more guitar-driven sound than the band has leaned into before.

thom yorke|harrowdown hill.fact: Thom Yorke's "Harrowdown Hill" was the first single from his 2006 solo debut The Eraser, reaching #23 on the UK singles chart - the song actually dates back to the sessions for Radiohead's Hail to the Thief, though Yorke felt it never quite worked as a Radiohead song.

buck meek|can i mend it?.fact: Buck Meek's "Can I Mend It?," from 2026's The Mirror, was produced by his Big Thief bandmate James Krivchenia - the album also features Adrianne Lenker on vocals, plus contributions from harpist Mary Lattimore and composer Alex Somers on synths.

grizzly bear|losing all sense.fact: Grizzly Bear's "Losing All Sense," from 2017's Painted Ruins, started as the oldest demo in the band's pile - Chris Taylor sped up its original guitar riff and added a bass line, then Daniel Rossen layered in melody, passing it back and forth for years before it took final shape. Its music video features actress Busy Philipps.

the smiths|this night has opened my eyes.fact: The Smiths' "This Night Has Opened My Eyes" was inspired by the play A Taste of Honey - Morrissey has said the play accounts for at least half of his reason for writing in the first place. The version released on 1984's Hatful of Hollow actually comes from a BBC Radio 1 John Peel session, not a proper studio single.

cheekface|life in a bag.fact: Cheekface's "Life in a Bag," from 2024's It's Sorted, was written by all three band members - Amanda Tannen, Greg Katz, and Mark Edwards - and produced by longtime collaborator Greg Cortez.

arlo parks|pegasus (feat. phoebe bridger.fact: Arlo Parks' "Pegasus," featuring Phoebe Bridgers, comes from 2023's My Soft Machine - it was produced by Paul Epworth (Adele, Florence and the Machine) alongside Brockhampton's Romil Hemnani and producer Baird.

the war on drugs|who's that.fact: The War on Drugs' "Who's That" was the band's first new recording since 2021's I Don't Live Here Anymore - recorded at Adam Granduciel's own warehouse studio in Burbank, with contributions from Spoon's Alex Fischel alongside the full War on Drugs lineup.

gang of four|paralysed.fact: Gang of Four's "Paralysed" opens 1981's Solid Gold, recorded at Abbey Road Studios in London - written by Andy Gill and Jon King, it's built around the memorable line "Paradise, if you can earn it."

tame impala|borderline.fact: Tame Impala's "Borderline" debuted live on Saturday Night Live in March 2019 before Kevin Parker had even finished writing the lyrics, ad-libbing much of it on the spot - listen closely after he sings "like a train" and you can hear an actual passing train in the mix.

wild pink|dead for a sec.fact: Wild Pink's "Dead for a Sec," from 2026's Still Coming Down, features MJ Lenderman harmonizing on the chorus and tearing into a Crazy Horse-style guitar solo over the outro - the album was recorded in just one week at Drop of Sun studios in Asheville with producer Alex Farrar.

chvrches|leave a trace.fact: Chvrches' "Leave a Trace" was the first single from 2015's Every Open Eye, self-produced by the band - Lauren Mayberry has called it a "middle finger mic-drop" of a song, about reaching the point in an argument where you realize nothing more is going to change. Rolling Stone later named it one of the best songs of 2015.
